slot.brief: Rank four alkyl halides (including allylic and aryl halides) in order of their rate of solvolysis via SN1.

stem: Arrange these compounds in decreasing order of their solvolysis rates via the $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism: tert-butyl bromide, allyl bromide, ethyl bromide and bromobenzene.
options: tert-Butyl bromide $>$ allyl bromide $>$ ethyl bromide $>$ bromobenzene
allyl bromide $>$ tert-butyl bromide $>$ ethyl bromide $>$ bromobenzene
tert-Butyl bromide $>$ ethyl bromide $>$ allyl bromide $>$ bromobenzene
bromobenzene $>$ tert-butyl bromide $>$ allyl bromide $>$ ethyl bromide

verdicts.working: SN1 rate follows carbocation stability: the resonance-stabilized allylic cation is favored over the tertiary-butyl cation; both are favored over the ethyl cation. Bromobenzene does not undergo ordinary SN1 ionization.
issues: Solvent and temperature are unspecified; the order assumes the standard qualitative SN1 comparison under common conditions.

verdicts.working: SN1 rate tracks carbocation stability: t-Bu+ (3°, hyperconjugation) > allyl+ (resonance-stabilized but primary; hydride affinity ~256 vs ~231 kcal/mol for t-Bu+) > Et+ (1°) >> Ph+ (aryl cation extremely unstable; C–Br has partial double-bond character, so bromobenzene is essentially inert to solvolysis). Hence tert-butyl > allyl > ethyl > bromobenzene.

working:
Rate follows carbocation stability: tertiary $>$ resonance-stabilised allylic $>$ primary. Bromobenzene does not undergo ordinary $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ solvolysis because forming a phenyl cation is highly unfavourable.

Independent check: SN1 rate tracks carbocation stability: t-Bu+ (3°, hyperconjugation) > allyl+ (resonance-stabilized but primary; hydride affinity ~256 vs ~231 kcal/mol for t-Bu+) > Et+ (1°) >> Ph+ (aryl cation extremely unstable; C–Br has partial double-bond character, so bromobenzene is essentially inert to solvolysis). Hence tert-butyl > allyl > ethyl > bromobenzene.
solution:
In an $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ reaction, the rate depends on carbocation stability: tertiary and resonance-stabilised carbocations form more readily than primary ones.
$$\text{tert-butyl}^+ > \text{allyl}^+ > \text{ethyl}^+ \gg \text{phenyl}^+$$
Bromobenzene is essentially inert because formation of a phenyl cation is highly unfavourable; hence the order is tert-butyl bromide $>$ allyl bromide $>$ ethyl bromide $>$ bromobenzene.
